title: Where Did Trick-Or-Treating Come From?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the origins and history of trick-or-treating, which they say developed in America in the twentieth century from older European traditions such as souling and mumming, and from Halloween pranking (including Mischief Night and Devil's Night in Detroit). They cover two competing theories: kids invented trick-or-treating as a form of extortion, or adults introduced treats to buy off kids' pranks, with Los Angeles and West Coast towns as likely origins. They trace its growth through the 1940s-1950s (Peanuts, Donald Duck cartoon, Ben Cooper costumes, Mars and UNICEF campaigns), the 1970s-1980s poisoned-candy scare (Ronald Clark O'Bryan-style hoaxes, the 1970 Detroit heroin incident, the Texas cyanide case), and modern parental over-involvement. They discuss free-range parenting views, the suburbs versus city debate, and trunk-or-treating as an adult-led replacement. The episode opens with personal banter and closes with a listener email correcting an earlier episode on paraphilias.
topics: Samira Kotwal Gangsters Pranksters and Trick or Treating

segments.title: Opening banter and trick-or-treating memories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Halloween, missing trick-or-treaters at their homes, costume memories, a recent Misfits concert, and the basic 'trick or treat' bargain.

segments.title: Pagan roots and Samhain
segments.summary: The hosts review Celtic harvest festivals and Samhain, the Hallow's Eve veil between living and dead, costumes meant to fool spirits, Halloween parades, and the pranking tradition blamed on fairies in Ireland.

segments.title: Souling, mumming and Mischief Night
segments.summary: The hosts describe European souling and mumming, where visitors received soul cakes or treats for prayers or performances, then survey regional names and pranks for the night before Halloween, including Devil's Night in Detroit and its arson problem and the Angels Night volunteer effort.

segments.title: Common Halloween pranks and rolling houses
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share anecdotes about pranks such as plastic forks in the yard, egging, the junior-senior egg fight, and toilet-papering (rolling) houses.

segments.title: Origins debate: kids invented it or adults did
segments.summary: The hosts recap the history and cite sociologist Samira Kawash. They present two theories: kids extorting treats through pranks, or adults offering treats to stop pranks. Los Angeles and West Coast towns are discussed as possible origins, with 1907 and 1919 early print evidence.
topics: Ruth Edna Kelley Book of Halloween

segments.title: Growth in the 1940s and 1950s
segments.summary: Trick-or-treating grew after the 1940s, dipped during World War Two sugar rationing, and rebounded after the war. Peanuts comic strip, a Donald Duck cartoon, Ben Cooper costumes, and Mars and UNICEF campaigns helped popularize it.

segments.title: Costume memories and special-needs blue pumpkins
segments.summary: Hosts share childhood and adult costume stories and discuss the blue pumpkin symbol for trick-or-treaters with special needs.

segments.title: Poisoned candy scare and urban legends
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1970 Halloween poisoning scare: a California dentist's laxative candy case in 1970 (noted as a 1970s event), the Texas cyanide case where a father poisoned his children for insurance, and the Detroit heroin incident. They say the scares increased parental anxiety and FDA candy-inspection advice.

segments.title: Free-range parenting and the danger debate
segments.summary: The hosts debate over-parenting versus under-parenting, citing Lenore Skenazy's view that trick-or-treating is a rehearsal for adulthood. They describe age cutoffs and the community's changing habits.

segments.title: Is trick-or-treating dying? Suburbs, cities and trunk-or-treating
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether trick-or-treating is declining, citing Julie Beck in The Atlantic on suburbs suiting trick-or-treating, and debate trunk-or-treating and church Halloween events as replacements.

segments.title: Closing remarks and listener mail on paraphilias
segments.summary: The hosts close with a plug for old Halloween slideshows, then read a listener email correcting an earlier paraphilia episode about BDSM and cross-dressing and suggesting kink culture as a topic.
